67.Option: TreeScan analyses can help officials focus limited investigative resources on emerging clusters and variants by automatically identifying statistically unusual patterns in genomic data across multiple levels of genetic relatedness and time periods.
67.Discussion_Source: By decreasing the reliance on time-consuming, manual laboratory data review and by simultaneously analysing data not only by genetic relatedness, but also by temporal clustering, TreeScan analyses can help officials to focus limited investigative resources on emerging clusters and variants.
Evidence: We conducted prospective analyses by using tree-temporal scan statistics [ 24 , 41 ] ( Table 1 ) in the free and open-source TreeScan TM software (Martin Kulldorff and Information Management Services, Inc., Calverton, Maryland). We searched for unusual increases that emerged over any recent time period at any node, from large phylogenetic branches to small groups of genetically indistinguishable isolates.

The maximum likelihood ratio for the observed dataset is ranked among those from the simulated runs under the null hypothesis, and a P -value is derived from this ranking as P = rank/(999 999 + 1) for the SARS-CoV-2 analyses [ 41 ]. For prospective analyses, a recurrence interval (RI) is calculated as the reciprocal of the P -value. For a weekly analysis frequency, this is further divided by 52 for the number of analyses per year. The RI represents the duration of weekly surveillance required for the expected number of clusters that are at least as unusual as the observed cluster to be equal to 1 by chance [ 42 ].
Investigators considered TreeScan results to be helpful in focusing staff attention and investigation resources.
TreeScan also provided coverage when external technological issues disrupted certain processes at PHL.
67.Rationale: The Passage Body describes a systematic, automated method—tree-temporal scan statistics implemented in TreeScan—that evaluates genomic data across a hierarchy of genetic relatedness (from broad lineages to closely related isolates) and over dynamic time windows. The method identifies statistically significant clusters by comparing observed case counts to expected counts under a null hypothesis of no temporal change in lineage proportions. The evidence shows that this approach operates in real time (weekly), processes large datasets quickly (4 minutes 15 seconds), and generates ranked shortlists of unusual nodes. Crucially, the text confirms that investigators found the results helpful in directing staff attention and resources, even during technical disruptions. This conclusion integrates the methodological design (simultaneous evaluation of genetic and temporal clustering), the computational efficiency, and the operational utility reported in the results, all of which are derived directly from the Passage Body. It is not a restatement of a numerical result or a limitation, but a high-level inference about the tool’s value in public health decision-making, satisfying the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements.

The evidence shows that specific leucocyte subsets—naive CD8+ T cells, exhausted cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, and granulocytes—accounted for a substantial proportion of the association between climate-related disaster exposure and biological aging acceleration (DNAmAgeAC), as measured by multiple epigenetic clock metrics. The mediation effects were both quantitatively significant and consistent across different aging markers, while other cell types (e.g., CD4+ T cells, plasma blasts) showed negligible mediation. This supports the inference that these specific immune cell types are key biological mediators in the pathway linking disaster exposure to accelerated aging. The conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the data and statistical analysis, satisfies the novelty requirement (not directly stated), and meets the derivability and complexity requirements by integrating multiple pieces of evidence and applying epidemiological reasoning about biological pathways.

79.Option: Paternal snus use starting in puberty, long before the offspring is conceived, may be a risk factor for respiratory and allergic outcomes in the offspring.
79.Discussion_Source: Our research indicates that paternal snus use starting in puberty, long before the offspring is conceived, may be a risk factor for respiratory and allergic outcomes in the offspring.
Evidence: In the paternal line ( n = 1090), 31% of the offspring had a father who reported using snus, with 8.2% having started in puberty ( Table 2 ).

After adjustment for paternal smoking and the offspring’s current smoking and other confounding factors, the offspring whose fathers started using snus in puberty had a higher risk of current allergic asthma [odds ratio (OR) 1.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.02–1.97], but not for non-allergic asthma. They also had increased risk of at least three asthma symptoms with allergy (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.10–1.21), chronic bronchitis (OR 2.17; 95% CI 1.04–4.54), and eczema (OR 1.45; 95%CI 1.27–1.65) ( Fig. 3 and Table 3 ).
No consistent risk increase was seen for these outcomes in association with father’s using snus only after puberty ( Table 3 ).

The difference between early- and later-onset exposure was very consistent in the main analyses and sensitivity analyses, and later-onset snus use was not identified as a risk to offspring health in our study.
79.Rationale: The Passage Body establishes a clear temporal sequence: paternal snus use initiated in puberty (≤15 years) is associated with increased risk of allergic asthma, chronic bronchitis, and eczema in offspring, while later-onset use is not. This association persists after adjusting for multiple confounders, including paternal and offspring smoking, and remains robust in sensitivity analyses. The evidence supports a causal inference based on temporality (exposure precedes outcome by years), consistency across analyses, and specificity (only early-onset exposure shows effect). The conclusion that paternal snus use during puberty—long before conception—may be a risk factor for offspring respiratory and allergic outcomes is directly supported by the data and is not explicitly stated in the Results or other sections. It integrates multiple findings (odds ratios, sensitivity analyses, temporal distinction) and reflects a key epidemiological inference about preconception risk factors, satisfying the complexity and derivability requirements.

80.Option: The health risks associated with temperature extremes are particularly pronounced among younger populations, with heat having a substantially greater impact on ambulance dispatches in individuals aged 10–19 years compared to cold, and this vulnerability is likely driven by behavioral factors such as increased outdoor activity and higher trauma rates.
80.Discussion_Source: This finding supports the conclusion that climate change and associated temperature increase constitute detrimental challenge for the health and wellbeing of young populations. 37 Limited ability to thermoregulate and a higher risk of dehydration or fever are presumable explanations that might play a role in babies and during childhood. 37–40 With increasing age towards adolescence and young adulthood, the possible range of explanations seems to be shifted more to behavioural factors. Children and adolescents tend to spend more time outdoors, leading to increased exposure to ambient temperatures. 40 Additionally, warmer weather has been linked to higher trauma rates independently of the effects of seasonal variation and this relationship is stronger in younger individuals than in adults. 41 Furthermore, both cold and hot ambient temperatures increase the risk of car accidents, 42 with young adults being particularly susceptible. 43 Moreover, young workers have been shown to be more vulnerable to heat-related 44–46 and cold-related 45 occupational injuries, possibly due to an inclination towards more physically demanding work in outdoor extreme weather conditions and lack of experience. 46 Additionally, there is evidence that elevated temperatures are associated with increased alcohol consumption and drug use, leading to subsequent health disorders, 47–49 which, in retrospect, can also lead to impaired thermoregulatory response. 50
Evidence: The heat-related risk was highest among young people (≤29 years) and then declined during the rest of life, with a non-significant effect of heat in the oldest age category (80+ years).

The contribution of heat to ambulance dispatches due to cardiovascular and respiratory causes was minor. On the other hand, the cold-attributable fraction exceeded 10% in both cases [10.82% (8.49 to 12.30) for cardiovascular and 10.79% (8.65 to 12.17) for respiratory, respectively].

The attributable fraction of ambulance dispatches due to heat in young adults (20–29 years) was >17 times greater than the cold-related attributable fraction [7.93% (7.28 to 8.50) vs. 0.45% (0.37 to 0.53)].
Children and adolescents tend to spend more time outdoors, leading to increased exposure to ambient temperatures.
Warmer weather has been linked to higher trauma rates independently of the effects of seasonal variation and this relationship is stronger in younger individuals than in adults.
Both cold and hot ambient temperatures increase the risk of car accidents, with young adults being particularly susceptible.

Young workers have been shown to be more vulnerable to heat-related and cold-related occupational injuries, possibly due to an inclination towards more physically demanding work in outdoor extreme weather conditions and lack of experience.
80.Rationale: The conclusion integrates multiple pieces of evidence from the Passage Body: (1) the age-specific risk pattern shows the highest heat-related risk in young people (≤29 years), with a sharp decline in older age groups; (2) the attributable fraction of heat-related dispatches in 10–19-year-olds is nearly 18 times higher than cold-related dispatches; (3) the cause-specific analysis shows minimal heat impact on cardiovascular/respiratory dispatches, suggesting non-cardiorespiratory causes (e.g., trauma, accidents) are driving the effect; and (4) the Discussion explicitly links this pattern to behavioral factors such as outdoor activity, trauma, car accidents, and occupational exposure in youth. This inference is not directly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived by combining the observed risk pattern with the proposed mechanisms in the Discussion, applying general epidemiological reasoning about age-related vulnerability and behavioral risk factors. The conclusion satisfies the novelty, derivability, and complexity requirements.

81.Option: IL-6, but not CRP, mediates the association between ACEs and LUTS in adolescence, suggesting a potential role for IL-6 trans-signalling in the biological pathway linking early-life adversity to lower urinary tract symptoms.
81.Discussion_Source: We found evidence that IL-6, but not CRP, mediates the association between ACE score and LUTS. This is contrary to our hypothesis given that IL-6 upregulates the synthesis of CRP and both have functional roles in immunity [ 44 ]. Despite their interrelationship, IL-6 and CRP have distinct signalling pathways as well as functional roles in absence of inflammation [ 45 ]. IL-6 is a pleiotropic cytokine operating through two distinct signalling pathways; classical and trans, the former of which is anti-inflammatory and results in the upregulation of CRP synthesis via signalling in hepatocytes [ 46 ]. The trans-signalling pathway is pro-inflammatory, acts upon all cells, and is associated with chronic inflammatory conditions [ 46 , 47 ]. It is plausible that, mechanistically, our results reflect the effects of IL-6 trans-signalling on the risk of developing LUTS, independently of the classic signalling pathway that upregulates CRP levels, but further research is needed to confirm this.
Evidence: There was weak evidence that the association between ACE score and any UI was mediated by IL-6 (OR NIE 1.03, 95% CI 1.00–1.06, PM 21%).
There was no evidence of mediating effects of CRP (Model 2) on the associations between ACE score and LUTS (see Supplementary Table S11 ) after accounting for IL-6 as an intermediate confounder.
A one-unit increase in log IL-6 was associated with an increase in the odds of any UI, daytime wetting, and nocturia in the adjusted models (Table 2).
There was strong evidence of an association between IL-6 and CRP [1.78 (78%), 95% CI 1.72–1.84 (adjusted); Supplementary Table S8].
Higher ACE scores were associated with increased odds of LUTS, e.g. a one-unit increase in the ACE score was associated with an increase in the odds of any UI [OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.03–1.30 (adjusted)].
81.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple pieces of evidence: (1) ACEs are associated with higher IL-6 levels but not CRP; (2) higher IL-6 levels are associated with increased odds of LUTS; (3) CRP is not associated with LUTS; (4) IL-6 mediates the ACE-LUTS relationship, but CRP does not. These findings, when combined with the established biological knowledge that IL-6 operates through two distinct pathways—classical (which upregulates CRP) and trans-signalling (pro-inflammatory)—allow for the inference that the mediating effect is likely due to IL-6 trans-signalling, not CRP production. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derivable by integrating the statistical results with general epidemiological and biological principles. It meets the novelty requirement (not stated in Results), the derivability requirement (based on data and known biology), and the complexity requirement (integrates exposure, mediator, outcome, and biological mechanism).

83.Option: The increase in incidence rates of DCIS among screening-aged women living in northern Italy resulted from an increased detection of the disease through the screening programme and from an uptrend in the risk of diagnosis independent of the programme.
83.Discussion_Source: The increase in incidence rates of DCIS among screening-aged women living in northern Italy resulted from an increased detection of the disease through the screening programme and from an uptrend in the risk of diagnosis independent of the programme.
Evidence: The APC analysis of time trend in incidence rates of DCIS in this screening-aged population showed that the birth cohort had a 2-fold effect. The nonlinear effect consisted of an increase in incidence for women born in 1933–42 and 1943–52, who have been targeted by the screening programme since 1997, and of a second increase for women born in 1963–72, first invited in 2010.

The linear effect consisted of a marked increase in the risk of DCIS for all successive birth cohorts or calendar periods of 4.0% per year, which was only partially attributable to the screening programme.

We estimated a relative increase in incidence of 8.9% (95% CI: 0.0%; 19.0%) every 5-year span of exposure to screening. The residual linear trend was estimated as an increase in incidence of 17.0% (95% CI: 4.9%; 30.4%) every 5-year calendar period.
83.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple lines of evidence: (1) the nonlinear cohort effect aligns precisely with the timing of screening invitations, indicating that screening caused increased detection; (2) a significant linear trend in incidence (4.0% per year) persists even after accounting for screening exposure; (3) the residual linear trend (17.0% every 5 years) is independent of screening and remains after adjusting for cumulative exposure. These findings, when integrated through epidemiological reasoning about confounding and effect decomposition in APC models, support the conclusion that the overall increase in DCIS incidence stems from both screening-driven detection and a separate, independent rise in diagnosis risk—whether due to improved detection methods or true increases in risk factors. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Passage Body but is logically derived from the statistical results and their interpretation.

84.Option: The age at onset of multimorbidity has declined over time, with younger generations reaching higher levels of multimorbidity at younger ages compared to previous generations.
84.Discussion_Source: Importantly, each generation seemed to attain different ages with higher multimorbidity prevalence than did the previous generation some years before, and women tended to fare worse than men.
Evidence: The prevalence of basic and complex multimorbidity increased steadily during the study period for women and men—except for the older cohort, which exhibited an inverted U trend.
Overall, the disease-accumulation trajectories among the different cohorts shown in Fig. 1 were S-shaped, with fast increases at young and adult ages, slowing down at older ages.

The median age at basic multimorbidity onset decreased between 2010 and 2021, from 47 to 45 years among women and from 48 to 45 among men (see Supplementary Fig. 2), and similar findings were observed for complex multimorbidity.

For instance, the prevalence of basic multimorbidity among women born between 1980 and 1989 was 37% when they reached the age of 31 years, but this prevalence increased to 47% among women who were born one decade later (i.e. between 1990 and 1999) when they reached the same age.
84.Rationale: The Passage Body provides multiple lines of evidence that younger cohorts develop multimorbidity at younger ages compared to older cohorts. First, the median age at onset of basic multimorbidity decreased from 47 to 45 years among women and from 48 to 45 years among men between 2010 and 2021. Second, a direct comparison shows that women born in 1990–1999 had a 47% prevalence of basic multimorbidity at age 31, compared to 37% for those born a decade earlier. These data, combined with the S-shaped disease-accumulation trajectories indicating faster increases in younger age groups, allow the logical inference that the age at onset of multimorbidity has declined over time. This conclusion is not explicitly stated in the Results but is derived from integrating temporal trends, cohort comparisons, and age-specific prevalence data using standard epidemiological reasoning about disease accumulation over the life course.
